content: Two peripheral community clinics in Chile, part of the National Health Service, conducted a study involving 554 children. These children were randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group 1, consisting of 276 children, received full-fat fortified powdered milk, while Group 2, with 278 children, received full-fat non-fortified powdered milk. Both types of milk were prepared by the mothers in a 10% weight/volume dilution, with the addition of 5% sucrose and typically 3% corn flour. The fortified milk contained 26% fat and was enriched with 15 mg of iron (as ferrous sulfate), 100 mg of ascorbic acid, 1500 IU of vitamin A, and 400 IU of vitamin D per 100 g of powder. Children were monitored every 15 days by the same group of physicians. The source of funding for this study was not disclosed. The risk of bias was assessed as follows: Random sequence generation and allocation concealment were not reported, leading to an unclear risk of selection bias. Baseline outcomes and characteristics, including birth weight, weight, and iron status, were similar between groups, indicating a low risk of confounding. Attrition bias was low, as the main reasons for participant dropout were migration and protocol violations, which were unlikely to bias the results. Performance bias was high due to the lack of blinding of participants and personnel. Detection bias was also high, as no blinding of outcome assessment was reported. Contamination risk and selective reporting were unclear, and no other biases were identified. In a separate double-blinded randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted in Malmö, Sweden, 54 healthy 11-month-old children were randomly assigned to one of four groups. Each group received different types of milk and dairy products with varying fat and protein content. All children were breastfed at birth, with breastfeeding rates declining over time, and none were breastfed by 12 months. The study was supported by various foundations and organizations, and the milk products were specially prepared for the study. The risk of bias in this study was assessed as follows: Random sequence generation and allocation concealment were not reported, leading to an unclear risk of selection bias. Baseline nutrient intakes and growth were similar among the four groups, indicating a low risk of confounding. Attrition bias was low, with 16 children excluded for reasons such as milk intolerance, protocol violations, or parental withdrawal. Performance bias was low, as parents and investigators were blinded to the type of milk and dairy products. Detection bias was high, as a dietitian aware of the randomization results controlled the children's records. Contamination risk was unclear, and selective reporting was high due to the small sample size. Another randomized placebo-controlled trial in New Zealand involved 225 healthy, non-anemic children aged 12-20 months. Participants were assigned to one of three groups: a red meat group, an iron-fortified milk group, or a non-fortified milk group. The intervention lasted 20 weeks, and outcomes included hemoglobin, serum ferritin, serum transferrin receptor, C-reactive protein, and body iron levels. Only the milk groups were used for this review. The fortified milk contained iron as ferrous sulfate, along with other vitamins and minerals. The risk of bias in this study was assessed as follows: Random sequence generation and allocation concealment were well-executed, resulting in a low risk of selection bias. Baseline characteristics, including age and sex, were similar between groups, indicating a low risk of confounding. Attrition bias was low, with minimal loss to follow-up. Performance bias was low, as the milk products were packaged identically, and laboratory analysts were blinded to group assignments. Detection bias was low, as the allocation code was only broken after data collection and analysis. Contamination risk and selective reporting were low, and no other biases were identified. A non-randomized retrospective case-control study in the Netherlands examined 99 children aged 1-6 years with recurrent respiratory symptoms. Participants were divided into two groups: one received dietary advice to consume whole milk, yogurt, and natural butter, while the other continued their usual consumption of semi-skimmed milk and low-fat margarine. The intervention lasted two months, and respiratory symptoms were the primary outcome. The source of funding was not mentioned. The risk of bias in this study was assessed as follows: Random sequence generation and allocation concealment were not used, resulting in a high risk of selection bias. Baseline outcomes and characteristics were not reported, leading to an unclear risk of confounding. Attrition bias, performance bias, and detection bias were all high due to the lack of blinding and incomplete reporting. Contamination risk and selective reporting were unclear, and no other biases were identified. Finally, a double-blinded RCT in Puebla, Mexico, involved 115 healthy children aged 10-30 months from a peri-urban community. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either fortified or non-fortified cow's milk for six months. The fortified milk contained iron, zinc, and ascorbic acid. Outcomes included hemoglobin, serum ferritin, soluble transferrin receptors, and C-reactive protein levels, as well as the prevalence of anemia. The study was supported by the Mexican Ministry of Social Development and the National Public Health Institute. The risk of bias in this study was assessed as follows: Random sequence generation was not reported, leading to a high risk of selection bias. Baseline characteristics, including age, weight, length, and energy intake, were similar between groups, indicating a low risk of confounding. Attrition bias was unclear, as the reasons for participant dropout were not fully reported. Performance bias was unclear, although the study was blinded to personnel. Contamination risk and selective reporting were low, and no other biases were identified.
